/grill-me One important feature I need for werk, including v0, is that Werk is able to work in different projects, including Werk itself. It should offer a project switcher somewhere at the top. The switcher should allow toggling between different project. There should be a plus button at the bottom of the list so I can select an arbitrary folder and add a project. Everything should be independent between the projects, only the UI should be shared. The project list should be persisted so when I add a project it stays on the list until I remove it.

When Werk runs in development mode, Werk itself should be present on the project list by default. 
Also, the modified code must live reload thanks to HMR. The updated code should affect not only the Werk project itself but all other projects.

card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Research, two rounds of real-app testing, and a direct repro of the one open correctness concern settle it. Two priorities settle the rest: productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.
subtree: 4 cards, 4 decided

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees the global object survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal harness shaped like werk's agent, pinned on the global object, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (an EADDRINUSE retry loop, then exit code 1). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): one guard clause in the server's start-up (a check, kept on the global object, that the server is not already running in this process) fixed both candidates identically. Both survive a real in-flight task through a source edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. Side effect worth knowing: this guard also means a hot reload stops applying code changes inside the start-up code - the tradeoff is 'my live session survives an edit' over 'my latest route-handler edit is live', which is correct for the original problem.

Runtime research (#werk-hmr:src4, Sept 2026): general research flagged one concrete objection to Bun as werk's runtime - oven-sh/bun #7716/#13811, open issues about SSE 'close' not firing reliably on client disconnect, which sounded like it hit werk's server directly.

Direct repro (#werk-hmr:src5): tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the exact version used throughout, and the one the research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to werk's actual live-stream handler and disconnected SSE clients both cleanly and via kill -9. close fired correctly every time, the client left the server's client list, no leak. The bug is real and filed, but does not reproduce for werk's specific pattern.

Decided: move werk's runtime to Bun (bun --hot). The one concrete correctness objection did not reproduce on werk's own code on the exact version tested (1.4.1). The remaining Bun tradeoffs are a values call, not a correctness one, and two priorities resolve them: bun build --compile is a real asset for productionizing werk as a shipped tool (Node's own SEA docs mark it 'Stability: 1.1 - Active development', a weaker position), and Bun's faster breaking-change cadence is an acceptable cost given agents do the upgrade work rather than a single unaided maintainer. #werk-hmr:opt2 records staying on Node as the rejected alternative; #werk-hmr:opt1 records the original Bun rejection, superseded once #werk-hmr:src5 tested it directly.

In v0, alignment before building is the accept gate, the plan's proposed answers and the build gates
why: No card names what v0 builds for alignment, and these three mechanisms already put every agent answer in front of the person before code.

v0 builds no separate alignment feature. Alignment before building is in v0 through these mechanisms:

- Every card, option, source and excerpt an agent adds waits for the person's accept (#werk-propose-new).

card werk-base-repo  [decided]
v0 is built in a new git repository whose main branch starts with zero files
why: A repository of its own shares no files, history or map state with the prototype, so nothing of the prototype can become v0's base.

The main line of every #werk build is the main branch of a new git repository, separate from the prototype's repository (#st-plan-main). Its first commit holds no files. The spec and the first tickets set up the project from that empty tree: the package files, the build and test targets, and the folder layout.

The prototype stays in its own repository. A builder may read it as a reference (#werk-base), but no build starts from it and nothing merges into it.

Each werk test runs on a fresh project directory with an empty map

The test harness gives a command-line test, a server test and a browser test the same thing: a fresh directory with a git repository and an empty map. The test writes its map with werk commands and reads the exit code and output of each command. A browser test serves that map on a port of its own. Facts I checked first:

- Today one server serves one project. The map path, chat, and session paths are fixed from the working directory when the process starts.
- `npm run dev` runs `bun --hot`, and the server is pinned on the global object so live sessions survive an edit (#werk-hmr, #werk-dev).
- v0 is a separate, empty repository (#werk-base-repo). No card covers multiple projects yet.

Round 1. These questions do not depend on each other.

❓ **Q1** - **Scope**: Where does this go? (a) A v0 requirement card only. (b) Build it in the prototype now, and add a v0 card. (c) Prototype only.

➡️ (b). You use the prototype every day. The v0 card gets the requirement, so v0 does not lose it.

❓ **Q2** - **Process model**: (a) One werk server process holds one context per project: map, chats, agents, and board. (b) One server process per project, with a shared UI shell in front.

➡️ (a). With one process, one HMR reload updates the code for all projects. Option (b) needs a reload in N processes and a proxy.

❓ **Q3** - **Background projects**: You switch from A to B while an agent turn runs in A. Does A's turn continue?

➡️ Yes. A switch changes only what the UI shows. Live chats, builds, and the diagram sync of A keep running. The switcher shows a "busy" dot on A.

❓ **Q4** - **Switch scope**: Is the current project (a) in the URL, so that each browser tab can show a different project, or (b) one global setting on the server?

➡️ (a). For example, `/p/<name>#card-id`. A card link then stays correct when you paste it into another project's chat.

❓ **Q5** - **The "+" folder picker**: A browser cannot give the server an absolute folder path. The options are:
(a) The server opens the native macOS folder dialog.
(b) A path text field that autocompletes from the server's file system.
(c) Both: (a), with (b) as the fallback.

➡️ (c). The native dialog is what you asked for. The text field still works when werk runs on a remote machine.

❓ **Q6** - **Adding a folder that has no map**: (a) Create an empty map in it. (b) Refuse it. Also: is a git repository required?

➡️ Create an empty map. Require a git repository, because builds, worktrees, and transcripts depend on git. If the folder has no git repository, werk offers `git init` and asks you first.

❓ **Q7** - **The project list**: (a) Where is it stored? (b) What does "remove" do?

➡️ (a) In a user-level file outside every project, for example `~/.config/werk/projects.json`. (b) Remove takes the project off the list only. It never deletes the project's `.werk/` folder.

❓ **Q8** - **"Werk itself" in dev mode**: Which folder is "werk": (a) the checkout whose source is running, or (b) the directory where you started the server? And is "dev mode" the same as `npm run dev`?

➡️ (a), and yes. With (a), werk appears in the list even when you start the server somewhere else. It is added as a default, not stored, so it does not stay after you stop using dev mode.

❓ **Q9** - **The agent's CLI in other projects**: The agent prompt says `node src/cli.ts`. That path exists only inside werk's own repository. In project X, the agent needs another way to reach werk's CLI. The options are:
(a) werk writes the absolute path of its CLI into the agent prompt.
(b) A `werk` binary on PATH.

➡️ (a). Each CLI call is a new process, so it always runs the current source. That covers "updated code affects all projects" for the CLI too.

Next: answer Q1–Q9. A one-line "ok" accepts my recommendation for that question. I add the cards when we agree on the whole design.

card vi-routes  [decided]
Each view has its own address, so Back and Forward move between places in that view
why: With the view kept outside the address, Back in Flow jumps to the previous map card. The Back button then means nothing in any view but the map, and a reload or a shared link can open the wrong view.

Addresses:

- `/map/<id>` — the map with that card open. `/map` opens the home card.
- `/flow` and `/flow/<id>` — Flow, scoped to the whole map or to that card's subtree.
- `/graph`, `/diagram`, `/board` — the other views.

The card id in an address is URL-encoded, so an id with a colon, such as an option or a source id, makes a valid address. An address that names a card that is not in the map, or is removed, opens a page that says so.

Back and Forward move through these addresses. A switch between views adds one entry. In Flow, a row click that goes one level deeper adds one entry, so Back goes up one level (#vi-flowtab-click).

Filters, sort order, and the Subtrees row setting stay out of the address. They are display settings, not places.

A `#id` link in a card or in the chat opens `/map/<id>` from any view. An old address `/#id` opens `/map/<id>`.

The server answers every view address with the app.

The open-card line in the chat (#werk-card-blind) names the card in the current address: the map card, or the Flow scope. A view with no card in its address keeps the last card named.

  -> refines         visual  The visual artifact is the primary medium
  <- alternative_to  vi-routes:opt0  Hash routes: #/map/<id>, #/flow/<id>
  <- alternative_to  vi-routes:opt1  Keep the view in browser storage and push a history entry on each view switch
  <- depends_on      vi-crumbs-place  Breadcrumbs sit in the sticky header, above the counts and the view tabs
  <- depends_on      vi-onview-root  The root view of the map is the page of the card #root, the same as any card page
  <- depends_on      vi-measure  Measure is a fifth tab for the pipeline and tool measures, beside Flow
  <- depends_on      werk-chat-no-card-line  A turn sent from the whole tree names the home card
  <- depends_on      vi-flowtab  Flow is a fourth tab beside the graph, the diagram, and the board
  <- depends_on      vi-board  A ticket board is a view beside the map, the graph, and the diagram
  <- depends_on      werk-card-blind  The open-card announcement has no recovery path once it drops from context
Options
  vi-routes:opt0  Hash routes: #/map/<id>, #/flow/<id>
    why not: They work with no server change, but the whole place is one fragment after the hash. A path such as /flow/<id> is an address a person reads, types, and shares as it is.
  vi-routes:opt1  Keep the view in browser storage and push a history entry on each view switch
    why not: Back would work, but the address still does not name the view. A reload or a shared link opens whatever view the browser last stored.

/**

 * `--input-format stream-json` / `--output-format stream-json` for agent.ts to run a turn,
 * and records what it was asked so a test can read it back.
 *
 * Steered by environment variables, read at spawn time:
 *
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_LOG      file: one JSON line per launch ({argv}) and per stdin line ({stdin})
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_MODE     ok (default) | crash | gone | ask | hang
 *                          ok    init, then one assistant reply and a result per user turn
 *                          crash read one turn, write FAKE_CLAUDE_STDERR, exit 1, no init
 *                          gone  with --resume: "No conversation found with session ID", exit 1;
 *                                without it: ok
 *                          ask   per user turn, one can_use_tool request; the answer is logged,
 *                                then the turn ends with a result
 *                          hang  init, then never finish a turn
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_SESSION  the session id init reports (default sess-<pid>)
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_STDERR   what crash writes (default "boom")
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_SUGGEST  JSON permission_suggestions for ask mode
 *
 * Launched with `--print <prompt>` and no stream-json input — the way sample.ts and
 * prototype.ts call it — it logs the launch and exits 0 with no output.

}
const out = (event: unknown) => process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(event) + '\n')

record({ argv, pid: process.pid })

if (!argv.includes('--input-format')) process.exit(0)
